The Burrito grunt Anisotremus interruptus is a demersal fish inhabiting rocky reefs and sandy bottoms along the eastern Pacific, where adult individuals exhibit a maximum recorded asymptotic total length of 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters], a size considerably larger than that of several related haemulid species occupying similar latitudes. Field surveys indicate that this species attains puberty upon reaching a total length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters], a threshold that reflects the sustained growth phase required before the onset of gonadal development. Young-of-the-year recruits emerge into the benthic juvenile population at an exceptionally small body size, with the estimated wet weight at birth being derived from egg diameter data and calculated as 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams]. This minute initial mass places the species among the smaller hatching-size grunts, consistent with a pelagic larval strategy reliant on planktonic food resources. Early life stages are characterized by rapid somatic growth under warm thermal conditions, allowing juveniles to quickly transition from vulnerable recruits to more robust sub-adults within their first year of benthic residency. Comparative data from related genera suggest that the high fecundity typical of the family partially compensates for the elevated mortality rates experienced during the early planktonic phase.

Reproductive output in Anisotremus interruptus is considerable, with mature females producing clutches at a frequency that sustains populations under typical environmental conditions. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate is realized through the combined action of clutch size and spawning frequency; females deposit approximately 6027 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 6027 eggs per spawning event] with individual spawning events occurring nearly every day [F_R_i = events occurring nearly every day] during peak reproductive activity. This high daily output, estimated from comparative life-history data for the congener Haemulon album, underscores an energetically demanding breeding strategy in which females channel substantial resources directly into gamete production. The warm thermal regime likely facilitates the rapid vitellogenesis and high metabolic turnover needed to sustain this level of reproductive investment, conditions that are typical of the shallow coastal waters the species inhabits. Post-spawning adults migrate to slightly deeper grounds, where they recuperate somatic condition before the next annual breeding cycle commences. The pattern of near-continuous daily spawning over the reproductive window is unusual among haemulids, many of which exhibit more distinct lunar or seasonal periodicity.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult Burrito grunt individuals reaches 4056 grams [Wwi = 4056 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established for the species that link the 51-centimeter asymptotic total length to a robust body mass characteristic of a moderately large demersal grunt. Sexual maturation does not occur, however, at the peak of this growth trajectory; individuals first become reproductively viable upon attaining a wet weight at puberty of 461 grams [Wwp = 461 grams], which corresponds to the previously noted total length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters]. This decoupling between the size at pubertal onset and the ultimate asymptotic size implies a prolonged adult stage during which individuals continue to allocate resources to somatic growth even after reproductive capability is established. Such a pattern is typical of many iteroparous teleosts, where early reproduction is possible well before maximum body size is approached, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation while still increasing future fecundity through continued growth. The body mass difference between pubertal and fully grown fish, amounting to more than an order of magnitude, highlights the considerable scope for post-maturation mass increase in this species and suggests that larger, older females make a disproportionately large contribution to annual egg production through both increased fecundity and extended spawning duration.

Maximum longevity records for Anisotremus interruptus indicate a lifespan of 17 years [am = 17 years] under natural conditions, as estimated from continuous field monitoring at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, exceeding that of many smaller-bodied haemulids, aligns with the species' moderate growth rate and late attainment of asymptotic size, a syndrome commonly associated with demersal fishes inhabiting relatively stable tropical environments. The warm thermal regime is near the upper end of the species' realized thermal niche, and at this temperature metabolic costs are elevated, yet the observed longevity suggests that Anisotremus interruptus maintains effective somatic maintenance and repair mechanisms throughout its adult life. Comparative analyses with related grunt species indicate that such a lifespan is sufficient to allow multiple years of reproductive output after pubertal onset, with older individuals likely accumulating greater lifetime fecundity through repeated annual spawning events. The capacity to survive for nearly two decades also has implications for population resilience, as overlapping generations buffer the species against recruitment failures in unfavorable years. Senescence in this species is thought to be gradual rather than catastrophic, with older adults showing reduced condition factor and lower fecundity before eventual mortality.

The transition from juvenile to adult in Anisotremus interruptus is gradual, with the onset of puberty at 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters] total length representing a developmental milestone rather than a sharp physiological cutoff. This pattern may reflect an adaptive compromise between the advantages of early breeding and the benefits of continued somatic investment, a trade-off that is particularly pronounced in long-lived species such as this one. The 17-year lifespan (17 years) [am = 17 years] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] provides an extended window for multiple reproductive seasons, allowing even slowly growing individuals to eventually approach the asymptotic length and achieve their full size potential. Understanding these life-history parameters is essential for informed fisheries management, as the species' relatively late maturation and slow growth render it vulnerable to overexploitation.
